rows.title: Meet 'Project 2029' — and its war on the annoyance economy
rows.standfirst: Remember Project 2025? Democrats are building their own governing blueprint, and one proposal takes aim at the "annoyance economy": robocalls, endless hold times, hidden fees and other everyday frustrations.

rows.title: We're in a renter's market (believe it or not)
rows.standfirst: Depends on where you live, but renters have a lot of power right now in the United States. What’s behind this trend and how might you be able to take advantage of the renters’ market at your next lease renewal.

rows.title: Hate food waste? 7 creative ways to turn your leftovers into a new meal
rows.standfirst: We asked our audience to share their favorite go-to recipes for leftovers. Here are seven dishes — like stuffed peppers and a biryani casserole — that can help you use up all your fridge scraps.

rows.title: Why the US is losing the drone war
rows.standfirst: The US defense industry is struggling to keep up with the revolution in cheap drones vs. expensive reusable military equipment.

rows.title: How to win a penalty shootout (with game theory)
rows.standfirst: Lionel Messi is arguably the greatest soccer scorer of all time. But when it comes to penalty kicks, Messi is merely average. Why? Maybe the answer involves game theory.

rows.title: But first, coffee: The drink that energized the American Revolution
rows.standfirst: Colonial Americans were drinking coffee long before they dumped tea into Boston Harbor or fought a war for independence. The establishments that served it were already brewing revolutionary ideas.

rows.title: A hot summer trend in the sharing economy? Rental swimming pools
rows.standfirst: The Airbnb-style company Swimply said there have been about 275,000 private pool reservations so far this year.

rows.title: Obama's new Presidential Center and his tricky relationship with the South Side
rows.standfirst: How do residents of the South Side of Chicago feel about their new neighbor: the Obama Presidential Center? A mixture of pride and excitement, tempered with some concerns about what it could do to housing affordability. On today’s show, we’re bringing you an episode from our friends at Code Switch on the new center and its relationship to the historically Black neighborhoods around it.

rows.title: Does the new Fed chair care about jobs?
rows.standfirst: Last month, new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh presided over his first interest rate decision and press conference … but he didn't talk much about maximum employment.

rows.title: Why Trump wants to rip up his own trade deal
rows.standfirst: During President Donald Trump’s first term, he touted the USMCA as the largest and most fair trade deal ever achieved. So why is he now talking about ‘terminating’ it?

rows.title: Can the Trump administration make college cheaper?
rows.standfirst: Will limiting how much students can borrow force schools to lower their prices?

rows.title: Inflation slowed sharply -- but it may not last
rows.standfirst: Annual inflation hit 3.5% in June, down from May's more than three-year high — but the resumption of the conflict with Iran threaten to push up inflation as energy costs once again spike.

rows.title: 'The Trojan Teddy Bear': The promise and peril of childhood in the age of AI
rows.standfirst: AI is moving beyond chatbots and into toys, dolls, and robots built to befriend children. A leading child-development expert says the technology offers real promise — but also risks crowding out the human relationships children need most.

rows.title: Can the internet survive AI summaries?
rows.standfirst: AI summaries are gaining traction and making the potential for a “zero click web” increasingly real. What does that mean for the internet as we know it today?

rows.title: Inflation has been creeping up. How are Americans feeling its effects?
rows.standfirst: By now, you've probably felt it: prices are up.

rows.title: States sue to stop Paramount-Warner Bros blockbuster merger
rows.standfirst: California is among the states suing to block Paramount from buying Warner Bros. Discovery in a Hollywood mega-merger that would unite some of the nation's largest movie studios and TV newsrooms.

rows.title: EV battery recycling has a math problem
rows.standfirst: For some electric vehicle batteries, it costs more to recycle them than they're worth. That creates all kinds of problems, which a new Colorado law aims to solve.

rows.title: Young people aren’t paying their car loans. We can help.
rows.standfirst: About one in 20 car loans made to young people are in serious delinquency. That’s the highest rate since the global financial crisis. Today on the show, former FDIC chair Sheila Bair answers young listeners' car buying questions.

rows.title: What a Monopoly importer learned when it tried to make things in the U.S.A.
rows.standfirst: After getting hit with tariffs for the imported board games he sells, Jonathan Silva decided to see if he could produce a version of his Monopoly game in the United States. This is what he learned.

rows.title: Justice Department subpoenas New York Times reporters over Air Force One reporting
rows.standfirst: The Times says federal agents turned up on the doorsteps of several of its journalists to force grand jury testimony next week over their coverage of the Air Force One plane gifted to Trump by Qatar.

rows.title: 'Steal This Story, Please!' puts journalist Amy Goodman in the spotlight
rows.standfirst: The independently distributed documentary follows the Democracy Now! journalist's reporting career and the independent media model she built over three decades.

rows.title: Seven allegedly fake Chanel bags vs The RealReal
rows.standfirst: Once upon a time, if you wanted to buy a luxury brand item secondhand (say, a Chanel handbag) you had to have an in. There was no easy way to find one. But over the past decade, the market for secondhand luxury goods has exploded. There are now many online resellers where you can shop for used and discounted luxury items. One big problem — how can you be sure if it’s real and authentic?

rows.title: Largest housing affordability bill in decades becomes law without Trump's signature
rows.standfirst: President Trump refused to sign the bill without Congress first passing his sweeping voter ID bill.

rows.title: Even Taco Tuesday could be more expensive as beef prices continue to rise
rows.standfirst: Beef prices are continuing to rise due to drought, low herd sizes and concerns about the new world screwworm in the United States, but business owners in Texas say that raising prices could drive away customers.

rows.title: SK Hynix to the moon, Gen-Z to their rooms, and Connecticut tax reform looms
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!).

rows.title: Gas prices are swinging. How to budget for volatility
rows.standfirst: Gas prices have fluctuated since the U.S. and Israel launched a war on Iran, which disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and left consumers unsure of what they'll pay at the pump.

rows.title: Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
rows.standfirst: President Donald Trump on Monday imposed 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, declaring that Canada has unfairly discriminated against American autos, alcohol and dairy products.

rows.title: The best economic ideas from around the world — Planet Money Summer School is back
rows.standfirst: Our free economics course for your ears is on a quest for great economics ideas.

rows.title: Amid nurse shortage, a university rolls out the welcome mat for men
rows.standfirst: Only about 1 in 8 nurses are men, but their share is growing. A strong job market for nurses and sustained efforts to recruit men into the field have made a difference, including in the South.

rows.title: Two Cities. Two chip plants. One affordability crisis.
rows.standfirst: The formerly sleepy economies of suburban Austin, Texas and Syracuse, NY are getting two new semiconductor chip plants. They’re bringing thousands of jobs and dollars to the area but while Austin’s housing market seems to be handling the change well, Syracuse is in the midst of an affordability crisis. On today’s show, why?

rows.title: Court ruling freezes Paramount-Warner Bros. merger for now
rows.standfirst: Paramount's owners were hoping they'd be firmly in control of rival Warner Bros. Discovery by the end of this week. Monday's temporary restraining order puts that plan on hold.

rows.title: Why doesn't the US have better sunscreen?
rows.standfirst: Why has the Food and Drug Administration taken so long to approve new sunscreens? Unlike the rest of the world, the FDA only just approved its first new ingredient in nearly three decades. We learn about a proposal to speed up drug and sunscreen innovation, and a skincare influencer who lobbied for change.

rows.title: The 2000s called. They want their digital camera back
rows.standfirst: Why are people who weren't born 25 years ago snapping up the digital camera of that era? Blame Taylor Swift, trend cycles, childhood nostalgia and smartphone fatigue.

rows.title: Can World Cup mania grow MLS in the U.S.?
rows.standfirst: As the World Cup comes to a close, so does a massive real-time experiment happening just around the edges. Major League Soccer – the top men’s professional soccer league in the U.S. and Canada – has been scrambling to take advantage of this once-in-a-generation opportunity when average American sports fans suddenly cared a lot about soccer.

rows.title: China signals possible return of U.S. trade privileges for Hong Kong
rows.standfirst: The decision comes two months after President Donald Trump met with Xi Jinping, potentially warming ties ahead of Xi's expected U.S. visit.

rows.title: Trump $1 coins hit the market. Experts say they not only buck norms, but break laws
rows.standfirst: President Trump's face appears on a new commemorative coin honoring the nation's 250th birthday, which went on sale this week. It's one of the many unusual places his likeness has popped up this year.

rows.title: Federal Reserve looks for 'secret sauce' behind a successful Wisconsin toolmaker
rows.standfirst: Business is booming for Snap-on, a Wisconsin company that has made tools for professional mechanics for more than a century. It recently got a fact-finding visit from the head of the Chicago Federal Reserve Bank.

rows.title: Kalshi says it's not a sportsbook even as World Cup bets surge
rows.standfirst: The betting site Kalshi emerged as a dominant sports betting platform during the World Cup. But the company avoids billions of dollars in taxes by insisting it is not a sports gambling operator.

rows.title: The Strait of Hormuz no-fee, China cuts down on pollution and IMAX's economic Odyssey
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!).

rows.title: Why the Pope wants to disarm AI
rows.standfirst: Over 100 years ago, Pope Leo XIII wrote a seminal letter encouraging workers to unionize in the face of industrialization. The current Pope Leo XIV in his seminal letter warned of an economic disruption from today that threatens workers - Artificial Intelligence.

rows.title: China's economy grows 4.3% in Q2, slowest since late 2022
rows.standfirst: Lagging consumer spending and business investment offset the boost from strong exports thanks partly to the boom in artificial intelligence.

rows.title: FIFA scraps controversial deal to sell stakes in World Cup to private investors
rows.standfirst: FIFA abandoned a plan to create a commercial venture and then sell stakes to minority investors, just days after unveiling it. The plan drew sharp condemnation — and a boycott from European nations.

rows.title: What makes a toy go viral
rows.standfirst: Squishy, slimy, fidgety toys are having a moment. But it’s more than just an anxiety-soothing, social-media fueled trend – these toys are reshaping how toys get made.

rows.title: Oil companies report sky-high profits thanks to wartime crude prices
rows.standfirst: Chevron reported its highest quarterly earnings ever. Shell had its second-biggest quarter, and ExxonMobil doubled its earnings compared with the same time last year.

rows.title: Mamdani markets, America bets, Gen Z drinks
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week!

rows.title: Mortgage rates hit their highest level in a year, driven by war and inflation concerns
rows.standfirst: The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6.66% on average Thursday.

rows.title: Are you choosing to stay single? We want to hear from you
rows.standfirst: Solo living, solo travel, and solo dining are all being embraced as more adults are choosing to remain single. Many Americans aren't interested in dating, and being single is a symbol of autonomy.

rows.title: European soccer leaders to boycott the World Cup in an unprecedented step
rows.standfirst: European soccer associations said they would boycott the World Cup unless FIFA reverses a controversial deal to sell minority stakes to the marquee soccer tournament.

rows.title: The economy slowed a bit -- but Americans continued to spend
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 1.5% in the spring, according to the Commerce Department. That's a modest slowdown from the previous quarter — but consumer spending picked up steam.

rows.title: The renter-owner wealth gap is wider than ever, as many are priced out of buying
rows.standfirst: Housing has long been the largest source of wealth for middle income families. But many renters cannot afford to buy as housing prices soar, which could fuel a generational divide.

rows.title: Trump’s new Truth Social plan: pay $100K
rows.standfirst: President Trump’s social media company, Truth Social, wants to sell investors early access to its posts. When Trump announces tariffs or new strikes on Iran, those milliseconds matter in the market. Is this corruption? Is this legal? And what does corruption mean for the U.S. economy?

rows.title: A divided Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady despite high inflation
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged Wednesday. Fed policymakers say they remain committed to curbing stubborn inflation.

rows.title: More Americans are going bankrupt. What does that mean?
rows.standfirst: The bankruptcy rate has risen about 48% between 2022 and 2025, although it's still below pre-pandemic levels.

rows.title: World Tour 4: How to beat the resource curse in Norway
rows.standfirst: Let’s call it the luxury of restraint. This is what enabled Norway to avoid the fate of so many other countries when they discovered oil and it changed the mix of their economy overnight.

rows.title: How to beat the resource curse in Norway (Summer School)
rows.standfirst: Let’s call it the luxury of restraint. This is what enabled Norway to avoid the fate of so many other countries when they discovered oil and it changed the mix of their economy overnight.

rows.title: Even Moore’s law can't save affordable tech
rows.standfirst: For decades, consumer tech like laptops and gaming systems got better AND cheaper. Memory shortages caused by the AI boom are making those lower prices a thing of the past.
